canonical_statement: This paper focuses on maximizing RAG accuracy under a low-latency budget by operating at a finer-grained level of information extracted in advance from text chunks.

CoinRAG shifts document-context encoding offline: each chunk is encoded once, and online inference slices query-relevant token spans from the precomputed chunk KV cache instead of re-encoding full retrieved text.
Offline nugget extraction represents each candidate nugget as a contiguous token span within its source chunk so that the corresponding contextualized KV slice can later be recovered.
The nugget extraction pipeline first accepts exact substring matches, otherwise performs fuzzy whole-word-span matching, and abandons candidates that do not meet the similarity threshold.
The implementation uses GPT-4o-mini for offline nugget extraction and accepts a fuzzy-matched candidate only when similarity is at least 0.7.
Online retrieval is two-stage: BGE-M3 first retrieves top-kc chunks, then ranks only the pre-extracted nuggets nested within those chunks and retains the top-k nuggets.
CoinRAG slices nugget KV states from a full-chunk encoding, so selected nugget tokens retain the contextual conditioning they had when the entire source chunk was encoded.
Contextualized nugget caches are concatenated with the system-prompt cache after RoPE position rotation, using an order-preserving contiguous position-alignment strategy to remove structural gaps.

The position offset for each nugget is computed from the system-prompt length plus the cumulative lengths of preceding selected nuggets, producing contiguous positions without changing model architecture.
Nugget-aware fine-tuning trains the model on the same non-contiguous cache-composition structure used at inference and minimizes cross-entropy on target answer tokens.
The empirical evaluation uses the LongBench HotpotQA, 2WikiMQA, and MuSiQue multi-document, multi-hop question-answering benchmarks.
The LongBench evaluation split used 200 questions for each of HotpotQA, 2WikiMQA, and MuSiQue.

population.label: LongBench evaluation questions: 200 each for HotpotQA, 2WikiMQA, and MuSiQue

canonical_statement: CoinRAG was compared with Standard RAG, CacheBlend, TurboRAG, and KVLink; Block-attention was omitted because the authors treated TurboRAG as an essentially identical chunk-level KV-cache-reuse design.
Answer quality was evaluated with token-level F1 score under a prompt that constrained the model to produce concise answers.

outcome.definition: Token-level lexical F1 score for concise QA outputs

canonical_statement: Efficiency was evaluated primarily with Time-to-First-Token (TTFT), defined as the time to construct the prefix context and process the query during prefill.

outcome.definition: Time to construct the prefix context and process the query during prefill

canonical_statement: Prefill context length in tokens was reported as a proxy for active KV-cache memory usage during long-context inference.

outcome.definition: Prefill context length in tokens used as a proxy for live KV-cache size

canonical_statement: The primary low-latency operating point was a P99 TTFT budget of 100 ms.
Offline nugget extraction used GPT-4o-mini on 512-token chunks, while online retrieval used BGE-M3 and answer generation used Qwen2-7B-Instruct.
CoinRAG was fine-tuned for one epoch over 277,280 training instances with an effective batch size of 16.
The top-k sweep used kc in {1,2,3,4,5,10,20,30,50} for chunk retrieval and k in {1,2,3,4,5,10,20,30,50,100,150,200} for CoinRAG nugget selection.

The answer-generation prompt prioritizes verbatim extraction from retrieved clues, then clue-grounded multi-hop inference, and permits internal parametric knowledge only when retrieved clues are not useful.

The illustrated online inference flow has four stages: chunk retrieval, nugget retrieval within the retrieved chunks, KV-slice loading and position-aligned stitching, and query-conditioned answer generation.
For the three evaluation corpora, each chunk was pre-encoded once into a full-context KV cache and stored on local NVMe storage for selective loading during inference.
The implementation stores each chunk cache as an independent file and asynchronously loads per-document caches; only the selected nugget token ranges are ultimately used by CoinRAG.
Evaluation and latency benchmarking were run on an NVIDIA L40S in bfloat16 precision; model training was performed on an RTX PRO 6000.
Under the P99 TTFT <=100 ms constraint, CoinRAG achieved the highest F1 score among Standard RAG, CacheBlend, TurboRAG, and KVLink on all three evaluated datasets.
Under the 100 ms P99 latency budget, CoinRAG averaged 41.7 F1 versus 39.6 for TurboRAG, a 5.3% relative improvement.

population.label: LongBench evaluation suite: HotpotQA, 2WikiMQA, and MuSiQue; 200 questions per dataset

canonical_statement: Under the 100 ms P99 latency budget, CoinRAG used an average active prefix length of 465 tokens versus 855 for TurboRAG, which the authors describe as 1.84x shorter.

population.label: LongBench evaluation suite: HotpotQA, 2WikiMQA, and MuSiQue; 200 questions per dataset

canonical_statement: On HotpotQA under the 100 ms P99 budget, CoinRAG achieved F1 51.4 versus 49.1 for TurboRAG.
On 2WikiMQA under the 100 ms P99 budget, CoinRAG achieved F1 42.4 versus 42.2 for TurboRAG.
On MuSiQue under the 100 ms P99 budget, CoinRAG achieved F1 31.4 versus 27.4 for TurboRAG.
Across the three datasets under the 100 ms budget, CoinRAG had mean TTFT 65 ms and average P99 TTFT 81 ms.

canonical_statement: Across both latency-budget and context-length-budget sweeps, CoinRAG established a stronger empirical accuracy-efficiency Pareto frontier than the evaluated baselines in the low-budget region.
Encoding selected nuggets in isolation instead of slicing contextualized KV states lowered peak F1 by 6.3 points on HotpotQA.

canonical_statement: Nugget-aware fine-tuning improved peak F1 by 11.3 points on HotpotQA compared with no nugget-aware fine-tuning.
Nugget-aware fine-tuning improved peak F1 by 6.3 points on 2WikiMQA compared with no nugget-aware fine-tuning.
Nugget-aware fine-tuning improved peak F1 by 6.4 points on MuSiQue compared with no nugget-aware fine-tuning.
Across the training and evaluation corpora, GPT-4o-mini proposed approximately 7.1 candidate nuggets per passage on average.
Training-corpus nugget extraction processed 950,221 unique passages and yielded 6.08 million nuggets at 99.9% validity.
Training-corpus nugget extraction via the GPT-4o-mini Batch API cost approximately $265-$325 as a one-time corpus-preparation cost.
Nugget extraction for the three evaluation corpora combined processed 5,681 passages, yielded about 277,000 nuggets, and cost under $2.
Building the complete chunk KV-cache store for all three evaluation corpora combined took under 30 minutes.

quantitative_result.effect_measure: upper bound on total construction time (minutes)

canonical_statement: Full chunk-cache disk storage was reported as 146 GB for HotpotQA, 75 GB for 2WikiMQA, and 173 GB for MuSiQue.
Nugget spans covered approximately 70% of chunk-token positions across the evaluation corpora, implying roughly a 30% disk-footprint reduction if only nugget-covered positions were retained.

concept.text: Token-position coverage and potential disk reduction

canonical_statement: For Qwen2-7B-Instruct in bfloat16, the KV cache for a single 512-token chunk occupied approximately 28 MB.

population.label: Qwen2-7B-Instruct, 28 layers, 4 KV heads, head dimension 128

canonical_statement: Nugget-aware fine-tuning required approximately 140 GPU-hours on a single RTX PRO 6000.
Nugget-aware fine-tuning had a reported peak GPU memory footprint of 75.8 GB.
CoinRAG incurs offline compute and disk-storage costs that scale with corpus size and assumes documents are static or infrequently updated enough for those one-time costs to be acceptable.
Precomputed KV caches are tightly coupled to the language-model checkpoint and positional architecture, so changing the backbone model requires document re-encoding.
Downstream answer quality is bounded by chunk-level and nugget-level retrieval recall; evidence that is not surfaced by retrieval cannot be recovered by the generator from the cached context.

Nuggets from different chunks do not attend to one another during their offline encoding, so CoinRAG retains the cross-chunk-attention limitation of chunk-level cache-reuse approaches such as TurboRAG.

The evaluation did not consider inter-query KV-cache reuse because it assumed limited online-cache capacity; the impact of repeated or overlapping retrieved documents across query traffic remains untested.
The evaluation is limited to single-shot multi-document QA on three LongBench benchmarks; conversational and repeated-query settings were left for future evaluation.
CoinRAG did not systematically evaluate prompt-injection susceptibility; cached malicious spans could still influence answer generation if retrieved.
Aggressive nugget slicing can amplify surface-entity biases or omit linking evidence needed for the intended multi-hop interpretation.
A HotpotQA success case showed a direct lexical match in which retrieved nuggets explicitly identified Pleiospilos as a flowering plant and the model returned the correct answer.

A HotpotQA success case showed semantic-only recovery: no retrieved nugget contained the literal title "It's Always Sunny in Philadelphia", but the model inferred it from plot cues about the Gang and Paddy's Pub.
A HotpotQA success case recovered "Atlantic Ocean" even though that literal answer was absent from retrieved text, using cues such as Atlantic blue crab and US East Coast geography.
A failure case returned Jupiter instead of Sun even though the highest-scoring nugget contained the correct answer, apparently because several other retrieved nuggets repeatedly mentioned Jupiter.
A failure case returned George Harrison rather than the canonical Bob Dylan answer after nugget extraction omitted the Traveling Wilburys roster and preserved Harrison-centric clues.
A failure case returned Lowell instead of Norman because retrieval surfaced the University of Oklahoma but not its city, while a nugget explicitly mentioned Lowell High School in Lowell, Michigan.

The authors conclude that CoinRAG establishes a new Pareto frontier for long-context RAG under an interactive 100 ms P99 TTFT budget by combining compact nugget-level cache reuse with improved answer quality.
The authors argue that, on average, the gains from removing noisy and unnecessary context outweigh the loss from missing some cross-chunk interactions, especially under tight latency budgets.
